prompt_title: Should Schools Teach Mindfulness?
text:
Schools should teach mindfulness, but they should do it carefully and realistically. Students today face a lot of pressure: grades, friendships, family problems, social media, sports and worries about the future. Many young people are told to “calm down” or “focus,” but they are not always taught how. Mindfulness can give them a simple way to pause, notice what they are feeling and respond instead of reacting.

I have tried mindfulness before, mostly through short breathing exercises. At first it felt awkward because my mind kept wandering. But after a few minutes, I noticed that the point was not to have a perfectly empty mind. The point was to notice distractions and gently return to the present. That small shift can be useful. It can help people feel less controlled by stress or anger.

In schools, mindfulness could be especially helpful before tests, after recess or during moments of conflict. A few minutes of quiet breathing or reflection might help students settle their bodies and minds. It could also teach emotional awareness, which is just as important as academic knowledge. If students can recognize when they are anxious, frustrated or overwhelmed, they may be better able to ask for help and make good choices.

However, mindfulness should not be treated as a cure for every problem. Schools should not use it as a way to ignore larger issues like too much homework, bullying, overcrowded classrooms or lack of mental health support. It should also not be forced in a way that makes students uncomfortable. Some students may dislike closing their eyes or sitting silently, and they should have options.

Overall, I think mindfulness has a place in schools if it is taught as a practical skill, not a requirement to feel happy all the time. Students deserve tools for handling stress, and mindfulness is one tool that can help them understand themselves better.

prompt_title: How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time
text:
We should be concerned about screen time during the pandemic, but not in the same way we might have been before. The pandemic changed the meaning of screens. They were no longer just tools for entertainment or distraction; they became classrooms, offices, meeting places, gyms, libraries and family dinner tables. For many people, a screen was the only safe way to keep life moving and to feel less alone.

Because of that, it does not make sense to treat all screen time as harmful. A child attending online school, a teenager video-chatting with friends, or a grandparent seeing grandchildren over FaceTime is not the same as someone scrolling endlessly through bad news at midnight. The real question is not how many hours we spend on screens, but what those hours are doing to our minds, bodies and relationships.

Still, we should not “get over it” completely. Excessive screen use can affect sleep, mood, attention and physical health. During the pandemic, many people felt trapped in a cycle of work, school, news and entertainment all happening on the same device. That can make it hard to rest. It can also blur the boundaries between public and private life, making people feel as if they are always available and never truly off duty.

The best approach is balance, not panic. We should accept that screens have been necessary and often beneficial, while also protecting time away from them. Families can take walks, eat meals without devices, set bedtime limits and encourage hobbies that do not involve scrolling. Adults need these boundaries just as much as children do.

The pandemic proved that screens are powerful tools, not enemies. They helped us learn, work and stay connected in a frightening time. But tools still need limits. We should be grateful for what screens made possible, while remembering that a healthy life also requires sleep, movement, face-to-face connection and quiet moments offline.

prompt_title: What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?

I also cringe at the “perfect minority friend” character, who exists only to give wise advice, suffer nobly, or make the main character look enlightened. That is not respect; it is decoration. The same goes for working-class characters who are always crude, rich characters who are always heartless, older people who are always helpless or out of touch, and teenagers who are always rebellious fools. Real people are more complicated than that. Some of the finest pupils I taught came from difficult homes and carried themselves with dignity. Some of the most privileged were kind and hardworking. Life does not fit neatly into such boxes.

Would I refuse to watch or read something because of an offensive portrayal? Yes, if the whole work seemed built on contempt. I do not believe every unpleasant character must be softened, nor do I think art should be scrubbed clean of discomfort. But there is a difference between showing prejudice and indulging in it. If a writer cannot be bothered to give human beings depth, then I can find better uses for my time. At my age, one becomes selective, and rightly so.

I also cringe at the “noble environmental native” stereotype, even when it seems positive. It turns Indigenous people into symbols of purity rather than living communities with diverse opinions, political struggles, scientific knowledge, and modern lives. A flattering stereotype is still a cage. Similarly, the “angry Black woman,” the “submissive Asian woman,” or the “predatory queer villain” can reinforce old patterns of suspicion and disrespect, even when a single story claims to be harmless.

Would I refuse to watch or read something because of this? Yes, sometimes. I do not think every flawed work must be avoided; older works can be examined critically, and even current stories may have value despite their failures. But if a portrayal is clearly dehumanizing, or if the creators seem uninterested in criticism, I am less willing to give it my time. Attention is a limited resource. I would rather spend mine on stories that recognize people as complicated ecosystems, not cardboard cutouts.

prompt_title: Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?

text:
I am not especially surprised that people sometimes feel more immediate pity for an injured dog than for an injured adult. A dog appears innocent to us. It cannot explain itself, defend itself in court, or be accused of having made poor choices. When we hear that an animal has been beaten, we picture helplessness. With adults, I think people often imagine complications: Was there a quarrel? Was drink involved? Was the person foolish or violent too? That may not be fair, but it is how the human mind often works.

There is also the matter of closeness. Many families treat pets as members of the household. A dog may greet you every morning, sit beside you in illness, and ask for very little beyond food, exercise, and affection. A foreign tourist, in the example, is an abstraction to many people. That does not make the tourist less valuable, but it may explain the emotional reaction.

Still, I do not think it is wrong to care about animal welfare while humans are suffering. A civilized society is judged partly by how it treats the weak, and animals are certainly among the weak. When I was teaching, I often told pupils that discipline is not merely obeying rules when someone is watching. It is learning self-control, decency, and responsibility. A boy who torments a cat or laughs at a hurt dog is not showing harmless mischief; he is revealing a defect of character that should be corrected.

However, our compassion must be properly ordered. Human life has a special dignity, and we should not neglect the hungry child, the lonely old person, or the victim of war because we find animal suffering easier to look at. It is sentimental and immature to weep over a stray puppy while ignoring the suffering neighbor next door.

The best answer is not to choose one compassion and discard the other. We should feed the poor, visit the sick, protect children, and also punish cruelty to animals. Kindness is not a limited supply, unless we allow it to become shallow feeling instead of steady duty.

prompt_title: Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?

text:
I do not think it is wrong to care deeply about animal welfare while humans are suffering. The mistake is assuming compassion is a fixed resource, as if concern for a beaten dog must be stolen from concern for a beaten person. In my experience, moral attention does not work that way. People who notice cruelty to animals are often also alert to other forms of harm, including poverty, violence and environmental injustice.

It is true that many people seem to respond more emotionally to animal suffering than to human suffering. One reason may be perceived innocence. A dog or a calf is not seen as responsible for its situation, while people often make quick, unfair judgments about other people’s choices, background or nationality. Distance matters too. A pet is familiar; a foreign tourist or a stranger in a news story may feel abstract. This does not make the reaction morally ideal, but it helps explain it.

As an environmental scientist, I also see human welfare and animal welfare as connected. Industrial pollution, habitat destruction, factory farming and climate change harm animals and people at the same time. A polluted river kills fish, but it may also poison drinking water and destroy livelihoods. Protecting wetlands helps birds and amphibians, but it also reduces flood risk for nearby communities. Reducing cruelty in food systems can improve animal lives, worker safety, public health and land use.

Still, priorities matter. If a child lacks clean water, medical care or food, that need is urgent. I would not defend spending lavishly on luxury services for pets while ignoring preventable human suffering. But basic animal welfare is not a luxury. The way a society treats vulnerable creatures reveals something about its habits of power and restraint.

The better question is not whether we should choose humans or animals. It is whether our concern is consistent, evidence-based and directed toward reducing suffering where we can. A humane society should be able to protect people without becoming indifferent to animals. In fact, learning to care across species may strengthen, not weaken, our capacity for justice.

prompt_title: Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
